Getting Started

Welcome to OSdev! Before starting making your very own OS you should be familiar with C and assembly (for your chosen architecture).

Development Enviroment

We recommend linux but any would work, for some topics on here (especially testing) linux is used as an example, we wont cover editors since that is your choice

Windows

The easiest path is WSL2 which runs a real linux kernel inside a lightweight hyperV VM and gives you access to standard Linux tools. If you want to avoid virtualization, MSYS2 provides a good Unix-like environment natively on Windows. You can also use Visual Sutdio and MSVC but keep in mind that MSVC does not support inline assembly on x86_64 targets.

Linux

Pick any distribution you are comfortable with. Later on, having IOMMU configured will be useful when testing drivers for real hardware

Emulators

QEMU is by far the best and standard emulator for osdev, Supporting GDB debugging, hardware virtualization, great architecture support and 100s of emulated & paravirtualized devices, on Windows it is a bit limited due to the OS but still supports many features. Choose Bochs if you want a cycle accurate x86_64 emulator, or Virtual Box / VMWare if you have specific needs, we recommend that you test these and choose which one you are the most comfortable using

Compilers & Assemblers

A cross compiler is recommended since your system compiler is made for userspace programs for your host OS, you can use GCC (x86_64-elf-gcc for example) or Clang with a bare metal target, you can compile a GCC cross compiler yourself or download a prebuilt toolchain. As said above, MSVC is another options. For an assembler we recommend you choose NASM.

BIOS or UEFI

Many will tell you to start with BIOS but modern hardware has phased out legacy BIOS in favor of UEFI. While BIOS drops you in 16bit mode and requires you to manually transition up to 64bit mode, UEFI hands your bootloader control in 64bit mode and gives you boot services which makes loading your kernel for example much easier. Unless you are intentionally targeting retro PCs, stick with UEFI.

Choosing Your Kernel Type

One of the earliest decisions you would make is choosing how much code will be in the kernel space (ring 0) and user space (ring 3)

Monolithic kernels are used by systems like Linux and BSD. In this design almost everything (memory managment, scheduler, filesystems, hardware drivers, etc) run inside kernel space, this avoids communication layers between these components. A downside is that if a bug (eg. null pointer derefrence) happens inside it will crash the entire machine

Microkernels Are opposite from monolithic kernels, the kernel is stripped to its bare minimum, thread scheduling, memory managment and Inter Process Communication (IPC), everything else (eg. drivers) run in usermode. This requires careful IPC design

Hybrid kernels, such as Windows NT kernel but they keep performance critical parts inside kernel space to avoid context switching

Hardware Support

Choosing this now is important when testing your os / using it on real hardware. Modern PCs have largely abandoned legacy standards like PS/2, old storage interfaces, and old graphics standards, while most people would tell to support this, remember that you will be implementing obsolete standards, if supporting older PCs these standards are a must to implement, we recommend that you read our topics from a legacy standard and a modern standard and see what suits your OS the most.
